text: Midnight. My office was two rooms at the top of a walk-up on Mulberry Street, and the second room was mostly for show.
Midnight. My office was a room over a tailor’s on Mulberry Street, with my name on the door in gold leaf that was coming off one letter at a time.
Midnight. The office was where I’d left it, at the top of four flights on Mulberry Street, which is the only thing about it you could count on.
Midnight, and the office on Mulberry Street was as quiet as an office gets when nobody is paying for it to be loud.
Midnight. My office was a desk, two chairs and a window on Mulberry Street, and the window was the only one of them with a view.
Somebody came up the stairs. Nobody comes up those stairs after midnight with good news; the good news waits for morning, like a gentleman.
Feet on the stairs, four flights of them, taken slowly. Nobody climbs four flights at midnight for the view.
There was a knock, and then the door opened before I’d said anything, which is how people knock when they’ve made up their minds.
The street door banged downstairs, and somebody started up. I put my feet down off the desk. It’s the only preparation I make.

Ten dollars came out of a pocket that had been saving it for something better. “Find out who. And get it back.”
I took the money. The case came with it, the way a cold comes with a wet night.
I took the money and my hat, in that order.
I took the money. It was the first good news of the night, and I was making the most of it.

Midnight. The office on Mulberry Street had one lamp, one chair worth sitting in and one detective, and the detective was in the worst repair of the three.
Midnight. I was in my office on Mulberry Street, going over the month’s bills by the desk lamp.
Midnight. The office on Mulberry Street was dark except for the desk lamp, and the street under the window had gone quiet.
Midnight. My office on Mulberry Street had my name on the door, a bottle in the drawer and the landlord’s bill under the bottle, where I could keep an eye on it.
The street door went downstairs, and somebody started up, taking the stairs slowly, like somebody not sure they were the right stairs.
Somebody knocked twice, politely, and then a third time, less politely.
I heard steps on the stairs, stopping on every landing to think it over.
A shape came up against the frosted glass of the door, and then a knock that didn’t want to be a knock.
Somebody was coming up. At this hour it’s either trouble or a client, and in my experience they climb at the same speed.
The stairs creaked all the way up, and then somebody stood outside my door long enough to change their mind and change it back.

I put the money in my wallet, where it looked lonely and slightly surprised.
I took the money and my coat, and turned off the lamp.
I took the money. By the end of the week it would belong to my landlord, but for tonight the two of us were getting along fine.
I folded the money into my pocket and reached for my hat.
I took the money and said I’d start tonight. It was already tonight, so for once I was on time.
I took the money, and the night along with it.
